blocks.text: Pop restores the parent prefix

Appending a candidate changes the shared path from the parent prefix P to the child path P + [candidate]. The recursive call must see that child path, but after it returns the parent loop must again see exactly P.
The final pop removes the element appended by this stack frame. Without it, the next sibling B would start from P + [A] and become P + [A, B] instead of P + [B].

The pop acts on the live path, not on detached snapshots already stored in results. It does not delete the candidate from the immutable input, and it provides no sorting guarantee; its sole job is to reverse this frame's append.

blocks.text: The visited mark lives for exactly one active route

After the current cell is validated, marking it prevents every descendant of this route from reusing it. Unmarking before those descendants finish would reopen the cell too early and allow a cycle within the same path.

Once all neighbor searches return, this route no longer owns the mark. Clearing it before returning restores the parent's visited set, so another sibling route or starting cell can use the cell independently.

Unmarking before recursion defeats the no-reuse rule for descendants. Never unmarking makes a path-local restriction global. Waiting until all starting cells finish leaks one route's state into unrelated searches and can suppress valid paths.

blocks.text: Undo depends on whether the parent was mutated
Explicit undo is necessary when a child changes an object that the parent or a later sibling will reuse. The inverse operation is what reconstructs the parent's pre-choice state.

If each child instead receives a fresh copy or immutable child version, the parent object is never changed. Returning from the call discards the child reference, so no pop or unmark is needed for that representation. The tradeoff is usually extra allocation, copying, or persistent-structure overhead.
A shared path, in-place board mark, or global assignment is visible to siblings after the child returns. Each therefore needs an inverse update unless the design changes to branch-local state.

blocks.text: Trace the leaked element
Let the parent path initially be P. Appending A produces P + [A]. Because the solver forgets to pop, returning from A's child leaves that exact path in memory.

The parent then appends sibling B to the contaminated path, producing P + [A, B]. Relative to the choices named in the prompt, B therefore inherits A followed by B, although the correct sibling path would be P + [B].

B alone is what correct restoration would produce. The path cannot be empty because both appends mutate it. A detached result snapshot is unrelated: the bug is in the live path reused by the recursive search.

blocks.text: Undo applies the inverse update
Suppose the parent enters with remainingTarget = R. Choosing x mutates the shared field to R - x, and the child evaluates its constraints using that reduced value.

After the child returns, adding x gives (R - x) + x = R. This restores the exact parent value before another candidate is tried. The inverse must match the actual mutation; restoring some convenient constant is not sufficient.

Subtracting again yields R - 2x and increases the error. Setting zero discards R unless it happened to be zero. Recomputing the result list changes an unrelated output structure and cannot restore the numeric branch field.

blocks.text: Short-circuit only after restoring observable input

The successful child proves that a solution exists, so the find-one search need not explore further siblings. That controls search coverage, but it does not cancel the public requirement that the caller receive its board unchanged.

Before this stack frame returns true, it must reverse every board or path mutation it owns. Each caller performs the same cleanup while success propagates upward. When the public call finally returns, all in-place marks have been removed and the success value is preserved.

Returning before cleanup exposes temporary marks to the caller. Clearing the success result confuses state restoration with result semantics. Exploring every remaining sibling ignores the stated find-one contract and adds work without improving correctness.

blocks.text: Snapshot and pop act on different objects
On completion, copying the live path creates a detached snapshot whose contents should survive later search mutations. The copy preserves an output value; it does not modify its source.

The live path still contains the completed branch's last choice. Popping that live path restores the parent prefix for sibling exploration, while the detached result remains unchanged. Collect-all solvers commonly need both operations.
Copying does not remove a source element. The result collection does not become candidate input, and a correct snapshot owns independent storage, so later popping the live path cannot delete it.

blocks.text: Restore the whole parent-state tuple
The branch state is the tuple (path, used flags, remainingTarget). A choice changes all three components, so the child receives a coordinated state describing the same selection.

Before the next sibling, every changed component must equal its pre-choice value: remove the path element, clear the corresponding used mark, and reverse the target update. Restoring only part of the tuple creates contradictions, such as an unmarked value that still appears in the path.

Used flags and remainingTarget remain mutated unless explicitly reversed or copied. The path and target would still describe the child. Failure is precisely when sibling exploration continues from the parent.

constraints: At depth i, a distinct copied path of length O(i) remains active.

blocks.text: Sum every copied prefix still alive

At depth i, the active call retains a distinct copied path of O(i) elements. Along a deepest active chain, paths of lengths proportional to 1, 2, ..., d coexist because none of those calls has returned.
Their total is 1 + 2 + ... + d = d(d + 1)/2, which is O(d²). This is simultaneous active space, not the number of nodes visited over the entire search.

With one shared mutable path, only O(d) path elements need remain active, plus recursion-frame and other state costs. That lower bound requires correct append-pop restoration instead of per-child path copies.

O(d) counts only one deepest path and ignores the shorter copies retained by ancestor calls. O(2^d) confuses search-tree width with storage on one active chain; inactive sibling branches are not simultaneously retained.
